advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Pin `AccountIdIdentity` Cloud parity against fixed expected tuples per state (or the pre-delegation decision table), not against `JiraBackend.resolve_assignee`, which now delegates to the same class.
evidence: test_user_identity_heldout.py:149-154: `expected = backend.outbound.resolve_assignee(local_value, remote_identity)` then `model = AccountIdIdentity(...)` / `assert model.resolve(...) == expected`

ABSENCE: both sides evaluate the same `AccountIdIdentity.resolve`; a regression in `_resolve` mutates `expected` and the assertion's LHS in lockstep, so no inequality can arise (regression-blindness, criterion d)

identity_model.py: `if trust_resolved_on_mismatch or is_account_id: return (resolved, True, is_account_id)` then `return (local_value, True, False)` — the branch `trust_resolved_on_mismatch=False` distinguishes Cloud from DC

test_user_identity_heldout.py:129-131: parity case `("a@x.com", ("a@x.com", True, False), {"account_id": "acct-9"})` uses resolved == local, so it cannot detect a wrong return of `resolved` vs `local_value`
ABSENCE: no case has Cloud resolver return a resolved value DIFFERENT from `local_value` with `is_account_id=False` to assert the local value is emitted (regression-blindness, criterion d)
advisory.finding: The parity test `test_account_id_identity_matches_the_live_cloud_backend_state_for_state` compares two code paths that now BOTH route through the same shared `_resolve` helper, so it can no longer detect a regression in the state machine it claims to pin. After this change `JiraBackend.resolve_assignee` delegates to `AccountIdIdentity(resolver=...).resolve` (backend.py:118), and the test's `model` is also `AccountIdIdentity(...).resolve`; any bug introduced into `_resolve` changes `expected` and `actual` identically, so the equality never breaks. The test docstring's claim ('if either implementation changes, the equality breaks') no longer holds because there is only one implementation.
merged_from: No test distinguishes the Cloud-only `trust_resolved_on_mismatch=False` branch: when the resolver is authoritative, returns a resolved value that MISMATCHES the remote, and `is_account_id=False`, `_resolve` must return the LOCAL value (not the resolved one) for Cloud, whereas DC returns the resolved value. The DC side of this divergence is pinned (test_data_center_resolves_to_a_username_and_is_never_an_account_id asserts `value == "jsmith"` on a mismatch), but the Cloud side is not: the parity `resolvable-mismatched` case uses `resolver_result=("a@x.com", True, False)` with `local_value="a@x.com"`, so resolved==local and the assertion cannot tell whether `local_value` or `resolved` was returned.
advisory.suggested_fix: Replace the live-backend `expected` with an explicit expected-tuple column in `_CLOUD_STATES` so a regression in `_resolve` breaks the equality.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Drop the AST `getattr`-scan of identity_model.py; rely on the behavioral anti-churn oracle (injected resolver → authoritative) which already forbids the defect it targets.
evidence: test_user_identity_heldout.py:64-73: the behavioral anti-churn oracle already asserts DC `authoritative is True` for an injected resolver
advisory.finding: `test_identity_models_discover_no_collaborator_by_getattr` asserts on the TEXT of the source under test rather than its behavior: it `ast.parse`s `identity_model.py` and fails if any `getattr` call node exists. This is source-grepping the unit under test (identity_model.py is executable source, not a non-executable instruction artifact, so the Rule-5 structural exception does not apply). The behavior it exists to protect — DC returns `authoritative=True` for a resolvable assignee via an injected resolver — is already covered behaviorally by `test_data_center_is_authoritative_for_a_resolvable_assignee`.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Replace the signature-name assertion with a behavioral check that constructing the model without a resolver raises (required dependency), rather than asserting the parameter is literally named `resolver`.
evidence: ABSENCE: the assertion targets the parameter's spelling, not any observable output; it would break on a rename with no behavior change (refactoring-violation, criterion a)
advisory.finding: `test_both_models_declare_the_resolver_as_a_constructor_parameter` asserts an internal parameter NAME via `inspect.signature(...).parameters` containing the literal string `'resolver'`. This is a change-detector: renaming the constructor parameter (e.g. `resolver`→`lookup`) is a behavior-preserving refactor that would break this test even though every observable resolution behavior is unchanged.
advisory.suggested_fix: Assert `with pytest.raises(TypeError): factory()` to prove the resolver is a required argument, independent of its name.
